description: The 613 Mitzvot; positive and negative commandments; ethical and ritual Mitzvot; Pikuach Nefesh.
content_html:
What Are the Mitzvot?

The word Mitzvot (singular: mitzvah) means “commandments.” Jewish tradition teaches that the Torah contains 613 commandments in total. These cover every aspect of Jewish life — from prayer and festival observance to diet, business ethics, social justice and family relationships. Observing the Mitzvot is how Jews live out their covenant relationship with G-d in everyday life. The Mitzvot are not seen as burdensome rules but as a gift — G-d’s guidance for living a holy and meaningful life.

Positive and Negative Commandments

The 613 Mitzvot are traditionally divided into two groups. Positive commandments (Hebrew: aseh, meaning “you shall”) are obligations to do something. There are 248 positive commandments. Examples include honoring parents, observing Shabbat and giving charity (tzedakah). Negative commandments (Hebrew: ta’ashe, meaning “you shall not”) are prohibitions. There are 365 negative commandments. Examples include not eating blood (Leviticus 7:26–27), not coveting another’s possessions, and not committing murder.

Deuteronomy 11:18–21 commands Jews to fix G-d’s words to their hearts and minds, to teach them to their children, and to bind them as signs on their hands — a passage that underpins the wearing of tefillin (phylacteries) and the fixing of mezuzot to doorposts. Numbers 15:37–41 commands the wearing of fringes (tzitzit) on garments as a reminder of the commandments. These physical practices turn daily life into a constant reminder of the covenant obligations.

Key Fact

Jewish tradition counts 613 Mitzvot in the Torah: 248 positive commandments (aseh — “you shall”) and 365 negative commandments (ta’ashe — “you shall not”). Different scholars have compiled slightly different lists, but the number 613 is the most widely accepted in rabbinic tradition.

Ethical and Ritual Mitzvot

The 613 Mitzvot can also be grouped into ethical Mitzvot and ritual Mitzvot. Ethical Mitzvot govern how Jews treat other people — they are fundamentally concerned with interpersonal relationships. The importance of interpersonal relationships as the principle underlying many ethical Mitzvot is a key theme in Jewish thought: commands about honesty in business, care for the poor and the stranger, fair wages and respect for elders all flow from the principle that all humans are created in the image of G-d (Genesis 1:27) and therefore deserve dignity. Ritual Mitzvot govern the relationship between a Jew and G-d — such as prayer, Shabbat observance, dietary laws (kashrut) and festival celebrations.

This distinction matters because some Mitzvot are fulfilled primarily through religious practice and worship, while others are fulfilled through moral conduct in daily life. However, in Jewish thought, the two categories are not separate: religious practice and ethical living reinforce each other. A person who keeps the dietary laws but treats others dishonestly is not living the fullness of Torah. Deuteronomy 30:19 expresses this holistic vision: “I have set before you life and death, blessings and curses. Now choose life.” This verse captures the idea that observing the Mitzvot — in all their dimensions — is the path of life and blessing.

Divine Providence refers to G-d’s ongoing care, guidance and oversight of the world. Jews believe that G-d is not absent after creation but remains actively involved. The Book of Jonah illustrates Divine Providence powerfully: G-d guides events — the storm, the great fish, the plant — to bring Jonah to fulfil his prophetic duty. Job 42:2 acknowledges: “I know that you can do all things; no purpose of yours can be thwarted.”

Yet Judaism also strongly affirms human free will. The Mitzvot only make sense if humans genuinely choose to obey or disobey them. Deuteronomy 30:19 (“choose life”) is a direct call to exercise free will. The tension between G-d’s providential knowledge and human freedom is a classic theme in Jewish philosophy, with thinkers like Maimonides arguing that G-d’s foreknowledge does not cancel human freedom, even if this is difficult to fully explain.

Pikuach Nefesh — The Sanctity of Life

Pikuach Nefesh is one of the most important moral principles in Judaism. It means literally “saving a soul” (or “watching over a life”) and establishes that the duty to save or preserve human life overrides nearly all other commandments. If keeping a Mitzvah would endanger a life, the Mitzvah must be set aside.

In practice, this means that on Shabbat — when work is normally forbidden — a doctor may (and must) work to save a life. An ill person may eat non-kosher food if that is all available to sustain them. The Talmud derives this principle partly from Leviticus 19:16 (“do not stand idly by the blood of your neighbour”) and partly from the general Torah teaching on the value of human life. Exodus 20:13 (“You shall not murder”) also establishes the sanctity of human life as a foundational principle.

Key Fact

Pikuach Nefesh (saving a soul) is the principle that preserving human life takes precedence over almost all other commandments. It means a Jew must break Shabbat restrictions, dietary laws or other Mitzvot if doing so is necessary to save a life. Only the prohibitions against murder, sexual immorality and idol worship cannot be overridden even to save a life.

Orthodox Jews regard all 613 Mitzvot as binding divine commands. They follow halachah (Jewish law) as determined by the Talmud and rabbinic rulings, and view the Mitzvot as G-d’s timeless instructions that cannot be changed or set aside by human preference.

Progressive (Reform) Jews believe the Mitzvot must be understood in historical context and may be reinterpreted or adapted for modern life. They tend to prioritise the ethical Mitzvot (justice, compassion, honesty) as the core of Jewish moral life, while treating some ritual Mitzvot as optional or symbolic. Conservative (Masorti) Jews take a middle position, accepting the binding nature of Jewish law but allowing careful, scholarly reinterpretation as times change. The existence of different scholarly lists of the 613 commandments (compiled by figures such as Maimonides) also shows that debate over the exact content of the Mitzvot has always been part of Jewish tradition.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain’ questions on the Mitzvot, be precise with terminology: use aseh for positive commandments and ta’ashe for negative, and always give examples of each. Pikuach Nefesh is a favourite exam topic — make sure you can explain both what it means and give a practical example (e.g. breaking Shabbat to save a life). A common error is to confuse ethical Mitzvot (between people) with ritual Mitzvot (between a Jew and G-d) — make sure you can distinguish them clearly. For 15-mark ‘Discuss’ questions, Orthodox vs Progressive views on the binding nature of the Mitzvot provide a strong two-sided argument. Accurate spelling of ‘Pikuach Nefesh,’ ‘Mitzvot,’ ‘halachah’ and ‘tzedakah’ is rewarded on extended responses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 613 Mitzvot are divided into 248 positive commandments (aseh — obligations to act) and 365 negative commandments (ta’ashe — prohibitions). They govern every aspect of Jewish life as an expression of the covenant relationship with G-d.
  • Ethical Mitzvot govern relationships between people; ritual Mitzvot govern the relationship with G-d. Jewish thought holds that both are essential and reinforce each other. Deuteronomy 30:19 calls Jews to ‘choose life’ by following the commandments.
  • Pikuach Nefesh (saving a soul) is the principle that preserving human life overrides nearly all other commandments. Orthodox Jews regard all Mitzvot as binding; Progressive Jews may adapt or prioritise ethical Mitzvot for modern life.

[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Jews mean by 'ethical Mitzvot' and 'ritual Mitzvot'.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: Ethical Mitzvot govern relationships between people, such as honesty, charity and care for the vulnerable (1 mark); ritual Mitzvot govern the relationship between a Jew and G-d, such as prayer, Shabbat and dietary laws (1 mark); both types are considered binding obligations from G-d rather than suggestions (1 mark); the two are interconnected — ethical and religious practice reinforce each other in Jewish thought (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the principle of Pikuach Nefesh affects Jewish life and practice.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Pikuach Nefesh allows (and requires) breaking Shabbat restrictions to save a life: a Jewish doctor must travel and work on Shabbat if a patient’s life is at risk, because the Torah principle of saving life (derived from Leviticus 19:16 — “do not stand idly by the blood of your neighbour”) takes precedence.
• Pikuach Nefesh permits an ill person to eat non-kosher food if that is the only food available to sustain their health, showing that dietary laws (important as they are) do not rank above preserving life.
• Pikuach Nefesh shows the Jewish belief that human life has supreme sanctity — rooted in Genesis 1:27 (humans created in G-d’s image) — and that preserving it is G-d’s will even when it requires temporary suspension of other commandments.
• Only three commandments cannot be overridden even to save a life: murder, sexual immorality and idol worship — showing that some moral absolutes remain even within the principle of Pikuach Nefesh.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per way — 1 for naming, 2 for explaining, 3 for developing with a source]

practice_questions.text: 'The ethical Mitzvot are more important than the ritual Mitzvot for Jewish life today.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Ethical Mitzvot (justice, charity, honesty) have universal moral value and shape how Jews relate to society; they are relevant in every context regardless of time or place.
• Progressive Jews emphasise ethical Mitzvot as the core of Torah, interpreting ritual Mitzvot as optional cultural expressions rather than binding divine commands.
• Pikuach Nefesh shows that even ritual commandments (like Shabbat) can be suspended for ethical reasons — suggesting ethics have a higher priority.
• Deuteronomy 30:19 (“choose life”) focuses on the moral dimension of choice rather than ritual practice.

Arguments against:
• Orthodox Jews regard all 613 Mitzvot as equally binding divine commands — there is no hierarchy between ethical and ritual obligations.
• Ritual Mitzvot (Shabbat, prayer, dietary laws) sustain Jewish identity, community cohesion and continuity across generations in a way that ethical principles alone cannot.
• Deuteronomy 11:18–21 and Numbers 15:37–41 command ritual practices (tefillin, tzitzit) as essential reminders of the covenant — not secondary to ethics.
• The Talmud consistently treats ritual and ethical Mitzvot as equally obligatory — both are expressions of love for G-d and other people.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Deuteronomy 30:19; Leviticus 19:16; Numbers 15:37–41; Pikuach Nefesh), explicit weighing of which argument is stronger, justified conclusion that recognises the interdependence of ethical and ritual Mitzvot.
Secure: Clear two-sided argument with some source reference; reasoned conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; limited source reference; simple conclusion.
Emerging: Only one perspective; no sources; minimal conclusion.
[15 marks — SPaG assessed on this response]

glossary_terms.definition: The commandments of the Torah; the 613 religious obligations given by G-d, governing all areas of Jewish life.
Positive commandments (aseh in Hebrew) — obligations to perform a specific action, such as lighting Shabbat candles or giving to charity.
Negative commandments (ta'ashe in Hebrew) — prohibitions against performing a specific action, such as eating non-kosher food or committing theft.
Commandments that govern relationships between people, such as honesty, charity and care for the vulnerable.
Commandments that govern the relationship between a Jew and G-d, such as keeping Shabbat, dietary laws and prayer.
The Jewish belief that G-d guides, sustains and oversees the created world and human history.
The God-given ability to make genuine choices between right and wrong, fundamental to moral responsibility in Jewish thought.
The Jewish principle that the obligation to preserve human life overrides almost all other commandments in the Torah.
